h: Getting the Most Out of a Day with the Big Cats
p: Big cats keep their own timetable. Tigers and snow leopards often spend the warmest part of the day stretched out somewhere shady, so it pays to see what keeper talks and feeds are on when you arrive and plan your loop around them. Catch the predators when they're up and pacing and it's a completely different show to a sleepy lump in the long grass. If you've got a camera, the quieter weekday mornings in term time are the ones to aim for.

With young children, think in short bursts rather than a forced march. Do a run of animals, stop for a snack, do another run. The mix of big hitters and smaller, cuter residents makes that easy, and it stops the classic mid-afternoon meltdown. Fans of One Zoo Three will spend half the day scanning for familiar faces, so be ready for some excited pointing. Allow most of a day if you want to see everything without rushing, and leave a little time at the end for the inevitable gift shop negotiations.

Getting there is straightforward. Broxbourne has a railway station on the line out of London Liverpool Street, which makes it doable without a car from much of north and east London, though you'll want a taxi or a lift for the last bit to the zoo. Drivers will find it close to the A10 and not far from the M25. If you've still got energy afterwards, the Lee Valley White Water Centre down the valley at Waltham Cross, built for the London 2012 Olympics canoe slalom, is a fun place to watch rafters getting soaked, and Hertford's old market town streets are a short drive north for a proper sit-down tea.
